utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Do I take it that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Reluctantly as it's a holiday everywhere else, Joanna Korner and Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham, Barbara Baruch, we're assisted today by Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. So let's proceed. Madam Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you. May it please the court. And I will try and please Ms. Korner as well with brevity in my continued cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Because she was upset about the holiday, working on a holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. We all are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I still have to stay at work even after court is finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For the court, Ms. Korner handed to me, and I believe has a copy for the court of the article which she believes that Mr. Osmanovic was referring to yesterday, and I would like to establish that with Mr. Osmanovic. I don't believe that the bailiff has -- do you have a copy of it as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, we'll hand them out now. I was going to use it in re-examination, but I let Ms. Baruch know that we found what we think is the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And for the record, I don't mind if it gets an OTP exhibit number. In fact, I usually prefer working from OTP exhibits. But I think for the record we need an exhibit number, so I will wait for one from the registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By our records, 1891.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So it is now Prosecution Exhibit P1891. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, can I say it again? It's 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I was just giving Mr. Osmanovic an opportunity to review P1959.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Baruch: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed it, Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is rather large. It's a big document, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it helps, it may help the witness. It's number 14 on the list that he needs to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I understand that that will be his particular number, but he I think deserves the opportunity to review it in its entirety, because I will question him about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you through, Mr. Osmanovic? And by the way, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the article you were talking about yesterday, the newspaper article that contained the list of names?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And even before you saw this list, I think you were telling the Court that you had received some gossip or hearsay, some rumour about this list from other people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from whom did you hear about the list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from my friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I have some names, please.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those friends who had heard it from their Serbian friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time you heard about it, it did not come from one person directly; it came from someone who told it to a Serb, who told it to a friend of yours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A friend of mine who spoke to his Serbian friend who had had an opportunity to personally see this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the friend, the name of the friend who reported it to you was what?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just need to understand something. When you say "I can't tell you," are you trying to tell me you cannot remember?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't put people into an awkward position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This has come up on previous occasions, and the rule that we have followed is that if the Trial Chamber is convinced or satisfied that this is so, the witness would be exempted from revealing the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Let me just understand it, Judge. I'm not disputing that's your ruling. But that would mean that the Defence could not speak with that particular person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask another question, then, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without revealing that name, although for the record, I would like it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I am not yet satisfied that we are exactly there as yet. So I want to know from the witness -- I mean, I expect you to put further question: Why would such a person be exposed to danger? What nationality is he or what ethnicity is he? And where does he live? And why would he be in danger? I'm saying he. It could be she. I mean, I'm sorry if I'm using gender discriminate language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I decided to come here and testify in an open session. A number of people who suffered torture, who were detained in concentration camps, who were mistreated, who were raped - I'm talking about females - simply do not want to -- they don't have the courage to come here and testify about the situations they went through, for various reasons, one of them being the fact that they either already returned to Teslic or they still intend to return there. My friends who told me about the existence of the list containing the names of Bosniaks and Croats, compiled by the Crisis Staff of Teslic municipality, they asked me not to identify the Serb who was at that moment in a very important position, because that person could be in danger. That person's safety and the safety of his family could be endangered. I can give you a very specific example to illustrate that. The owner of this independent newspaper decided to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to in any event object to the relevance of the question, as to why it's necessary for the witness to give the name of the person who told him that this list was in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the witness said that he was aware of this list before it was ever published in this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So obviously the question that has been put is to test his credibility as to that, whether this was -- what he's telling us was information that he received when he actually saw it in the paper or it's true that he received the information at the time by a Serb. So this is why. But I am not going to allow the -- or allow the witness to reveal the name of his informer. So we might as well proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: My next question was going to be with regard to the particular Serb who claims that he saw it. And I believe his response would go directly to my next question as well. But I think it's very important, as he has attributed a source for this list, that would be very surprising and unusual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have had Serb witnesses coming over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Not that it was a Serb who started the information travelling, but the source of the list I think is very important. And if you let me, I'll just ask Mr. Osmanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead. I'm not restricting you in any way. But I will protect the identity of people who might possibly be in danger, given the circumstances surrounding the activities and events that we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, it was generally, in 1992, and I think you said you learned of this list in May of 1992, a time of battles, quite close to the area of Teslic, and strong feelings and aggressive feelings on both sides; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Both sides. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there were suspicions in terms of those people who wanted to secede from the former Yugoslavia and those people who wanted to remain within the former Yugoslavia. They were suspicious of each other; would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, Yugoslavia was not at the limelight. The question of survival for common people in Teslic was not that important. On the one hand, there were Bosniaks and Croats who saw what was going on. They were disarmed, and the only possibility they had was to organise themselves. On the other hand, you had people of other ethnicity who controlled police, the army, and the paramilitary units, and the only thing that Bosniaks and Croats had in mind was how to resolve the situation peacefully, how to avoid bloodshed. Nobody paid much attention to the survival of Yugoslavia. The main focus was how to survive, how to protect the safety of one's family and one's own safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with your analysis that nobody was concerned with the survival of the former Yugoslavia. It appears to me that you're answering a different question than I asked, and I'll try to make it more simple for you. The non-Serbs at the time were very suspicious of Serbs in the area of Teslic; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, they lost confidence in the Serbs who held offices in the police, in the army, and in the civilian structures of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will you agree with me as well that the civilian structures of the municipality were also suspicious of the motives of non-Serbs in the area?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be your position here in Court that the Serbs were very trusting and confident that the non-Serbs in the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] He didn't say that. He said he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He said he doesn't know. He won't answer for the Serb side. That's the message.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you see a list like this, a list that now has the exhibit number P1959, do you not recognise it as some kind of security report with regard to famous and important non-Serbs who would have been residing in the area of Teslic, about whom Serbs may have been suspicious?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I don't know what you mean when you say "safety." Here, one could talk about the security organs paying a lot of attention to the safety of people and that they did make a list of the people that may have been suspicious. However, the organs that were in charge of security in Teslic municipality should have also listed Serbs. What raises concern is the fact that the people who are here on the list, over 90 per cent of them are people who are held in the highest esteem among the Bosniaks. Those are businessmen, teachers, professors, people in a very high esteem who had never had any problems with the law before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday you had my full admiration for answering the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Today you are answering anything but the question. Please stick to the questions that are put to you and try to answer them simply, in simple terms. The question, if I were to rephrase it myself, is a very simple one. Looking at this list and taking that it did exist at the time that we are being told that it did, wouldn't that mean that the Serb authorities had the suspicion that the people -- the persons appearing on this list constituted a threat to the security of the Serbian people? This is the question. That therefore, there was no trust or there was lack of trust between -- from the Serbian side vis-a-vis the Croat and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May I just add one thing to that, Your Honour? Because, for example, in number 29, they say "quiet, not prominent, and so far still a loyal citizen." And for I think at least one or two others, they say similar things. And so my feeling is it would be a list of people who are non-Serbs that they felt were important to know what they were up to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but whatever Mr. Baruch is feeling is neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Ms. Korner. So objection -- let him answer the question as I rephrased it, and then if you want you ask him further questions, but first he tells me whether he agrees that this list basically means that the Serbian authorities did not trust or had their own suspicion on the persons appearing on this list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Crisis Staff, which compiled the list, probably thought that these persons on the list might present a certain threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Osmanovic. And now I would direct your attention to number 29, and then on page 5 in the second list, number 2 and number 3 and number 4, there are also people on the list who it would be indicated in some manner or other would not pose a threat to the Serbs in official position in Teslic. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so yesterday, when you imputed the sinister meaning to the list having been written, you said there were people to be killed, people to be interrogated, people to be abused. I see no sign on that list that anyone on it should be liquidated. And if you disagree with that, can you point me to the area of this list that leads you to disagreement.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you start from number 4, the copy of Nezavisne Novine says Rasim Galijasevic. It says peacemaker, did a great deal to pacify Muslims, enjoys great prestige, a negotiator with the SDA in Tesanj. Have you found him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Number 4 in the second part of the list. Thank you. Is that what leads you --

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat. It says: Peacemaker. Rasim Galijasevic ended up in a camp and we do not know what happened to this peacemaker to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question was not with regard to what happened to the people on the list, but you said that the list was devised by the Crisis Staff for liquidation. And I just want to make sure that we can agree on at least one basic thing about this list: This list does not indicate in any way that a person should be liquidated, does it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Crisis Staff had compiled a list of prominent Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats, and it was thought that some people should be liquidated, some detained, some deported, and I said it accurately yesterday. And it is quite easy to understand that the Crisis Staff, in the written documents, could not really put liquidate against this or some other name or who should be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But you see, Mr. Osmanovic, it's my job to find out, when you make a statement with regard to liquidation, whether that was something you concluded or you thought other people were thinking, or if the list itself said it, and that's why I've questioned you about it today, okay? So can we agree here in Court today that the list that existed, which by the way does not - and tell me if I'm wrong - it does not say anything about preparation by the Crisis Staff itself. That list did not say to liquidate anybody. Can we agree about that? I think we do; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what about my subquestion, which was about the Crisis Staff? This particular list does not indicate that anybody created it as part of the official functioning that is compiled by the Crisis Staff, and point out any place where you believe that I'm incorrect about it, that it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. says it on the document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that the introduction to this text says with sketches of portraits of eminent Bosniaks and Croats from the area about whom the party leaders have established that they pose a threat to the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Baruch, may I just point out to you the title of this report, which, according to the English translation that I have, says that one of the criteria used by the people who compiled the execution lists was the colour of ceramic tiles in bathrooms, all distinguished non-Serbs in Teslic were targeted. So the witness is not the only one who has come to the conclusion that this was indeed an execution list, in case you want to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I come from a jurisdiction where newspapers are distrusted, and I have a feeling that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Me too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: -- that Mr. Osmanovic - and the author is blank, at least on my English copy - could not speak for -- or perhaps he does know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, do you know who the reporter was, the person who created the story?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday in my presentation I said that I had heard about such a list and that I had never seen it, I mean not in its original, that I only saw it in the Nezavisne Novine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is: Do you know who the writer, the author of this was? Okay. So we have an unknown author from a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? If it helps Ms. Baruch, I know exactly, because we've got the whole series of articles, how this was written and who wrote it. And indeed the witness alluded to it yesterday which is why knew where to go and look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My intervention, Ms. Korner, very simply put was Ms. Baruch was presenting the witness with a kind of surprise that he was drawing the conclusion that this was a hit list or an execution list. And she was suggesting that there is nothing on the face of the document itself that indicated that -- or actually I was just pointing out that the headline itself considers this list as an execution list. And I pointed that out in case she wanted to put further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I accept. I'm not sure we're pursuing this with much success. It doesn't say it on the list. It's just a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The only relevance -- the reason why I'm allowing this series of questions is the following: Because it may be important to establish whether it's true that this list existed at the time of the Crisis Staff, that is, in May of 1992, or whether it's just a fabrication that came up later and the witness is saying that he knew about it before. So this is basically it, and you will appreciate that I as a judge, I have to behave in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honours are unaware because it hasn't been handed up. We have an original of this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Handwritten, and I was going to put it in -- it was given to Ms. Baruch and she hasn't got it yet. Because there's no suggestion the witness ever saw it before but it is here and I'm going to put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Baruch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, did you ever see a handwritten list from which this typed or printed list was printed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he told us yesterday that he never saw the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Told about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on you became president of a War Presidency in Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the war president, did you have someone who was in charge of security information, of investigating what was going on and reporting to you important facts that might affect the security of your war president or your presidency or your cause? Did you have such people?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People were not giving you intelligence information when you were the president of the War Presidency in Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I explained what was the role of the War Presidency which didn't have territory of its own. We were primarily responsible for assisting the civilian population in various humanitarian actions, coordinating it with the Red Cross, Merhamet, and so on and so forth. Our duty was also to provide coordination for people expelled from Teslic with other municipalities, that is, with Tesanj, Maglaj, and see that they be accommodated there. As a War Presidency, we were not a presidency which had a territory of its own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that you didn't have your own territory. But what you have just said ignores what you wrote on page 10 of your original statement with regard to -- I'm sorry. The date of this statement being -- I don't want to get confused with the way we write dates. Was that July 12th of 2000? In which you explained that the War Presidency organised those who fled from Teslic municipality and also formed a military unit consisting of 1.000 people. So you were not merely involved in social action and social welfare of the refugees; you were also involved in military matters, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We helped bodies which were responsible for mobilisation, because there was the civilian population from the municipality of Teslic and we helped them to become incorporated in our brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So using more clear language, you organised combatants. And for that purpose, didn't you also gather intelligence with regard to what was going on in the area of Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I received came, by and large, from people who, at different times, came from the territory of the Teslic municipality, that is, through exchanges, and they talked to me and told me about things that were going on in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I'm getting a little bit irritated now. Please try to answer the question. And I know that you are in a position to answer the question. The question was not whether you, as president of this War Presidency, received information from refugees arriving from Teslic, but whether the War Presidency itself, once that you admit in your statement that it also formed a military unit consisting of 1.000 people, whether you stand by your statement that it did not have an intelligence-gathering organisation within it or that it didn't have the usual net of informers that kept it going. It's being put to you that it is very unlikely and hardly credible that a War Presidency that also forms a military unit and organises the people who fled from Teslic would do so without having within its fold, within its organisation, an intelligence-gathering section.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I have to repeat those things. Yes, we were a War Presidency, appointed by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we were duty-bound to provide the continuity of authority in a way, but we didn't have the jurisdiction, such as was exercised by those war presidencies which had their own territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I will continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, you said that you spoke with, or sometimes we use the word "debrief." You spoke with refugees from Teslic, and my question to you is: Did you write down reports with regard to what they told you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you direct them to somebody else who would debrief them and write a written report with regard to what they told you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of work was done by the public security station in Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were familiar with the public security section in Tesanj, and they kept such records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question: Was the public security department in this town represented on the War Presidency or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm interested a little bit in this army that you said consisted of a thousand men, of refugees from Teslic. It would seem to me that you must have had help from an outside force. I mean, you couldn't have done that solely with refugees from Teslic, did you, or the people you worked with?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Help with what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help with manpower, with money, with gathering weapons. Did you have assistance from an outside source with that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A considerable number of our people who had been expelled from Teslic turned up abroad, in Germany, or here in the Netherlands, and they organised their homeland clubs to help. So they helped the War Presidency to meet, as best it could, the civilian needs of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I'm talking about the civilian needs. Now I'm talking about the military needs. Did you have assistance with money and guns and intelligence, for example, from -- I think it's called the ABiH, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the army from Croatia, or by fighters from other countries, from other Muslim countries? Did you have that kind of assistance with this brigade of a thousand men?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade or in the early days the Territorial Defence of Teslic, which then grew into 43rd Teslic Brigade, and it was part of the system of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and incorporated in the core operative group and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were the members of this military unit paid? Did they receive remuneration to be part of the military unit? And if yes, where did the money come from? That's number one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number two: Were they supplied with guns or with weapons? And if they were, where did the weapons come from? Who supplied them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the early days, our unit had no weapons at all, apart from a few hunting rifles. However, after the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina came of age and after some barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army were blocked, such as those in Zenica or in Central Bosnia, and then weapons began to arrive in our brigade too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you got weapons in time as this organisation developed, and you've told the Judge that none of the people were paid. I assume you mean salaries. They were all volunteers, is that right, throughout the time that it was organised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the initial period, at least.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to know if I understood it correctly. What about a place to live and food and care for their families? Was that the social welfare programmes that the War Presidency was involved in, taking care of those needs of the people who were in this thousand-man brigade? Did you do that? Food, clothing, stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So money was not handed to them, but their needs were taken care of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I am finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, I have just a few more questions. One area is about the Banja Luka alliance for the municipality of Teslic. Yesterday you told us that in terms of health care, people went to medical treatment, to Doboj, in the hospital of Doboj, and traditionally, that association for Teslic was for -- was with Doboj, but that the new government of Teslic wanted -- Mr. Perisic wanted and eventually the new government of Teslic allied with Banja Luka. I'd like to explore that a little bit with you. Banja Luka was about twice as big as Teslic, isn't it, back in 1991/1992 -- as Doboj, sorry.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the financial arrangements, even in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the wars broke out, those financial arrangements would -- for that entire area, Doboj and Teslic and Banja Luka, they all went through Banja Luka historically, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the primary centre for financial matters in the region, went through Banja Luka, didn't they, even in 1990, as well as 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Banja Luka was only a centre of a region, just as Doboj was the centre of another region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then perhaps I'm wrong, and you can correct me if I am. I thought that the money, the financial arrangements for medical care, not the hospitals, but the money for that, and the money for pensions and the money for salaries would all travel through Banja Luka to get to Doboj, to get to Teslic eventually. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 1992, that is simply how it was not. You obviously ignore the organisation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. Its organisation was territorial. Teslic was under Doboj, and all the funds from the public auditing service went through Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "went through Doboj," do you mean it went from Banja Luka to Doboj and then to Teslic? No? Okay. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I accept your answer. In 1992, would you agree with me, after April of 1992, the funds came through Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that decision which was taken by the Municipal Assembly of Teslic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992, the road to Doboj was an unsafe road; that is, you would have to go through the -- for a person from the Republic of Srpska, you would have to go through areas controlled by armies aligned with the BiH; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have -- you need to be more concrete. 1992, but which month?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about April of 1992, maybe even April 6th of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right up until the 1st of May, 1st, 2nd, 3rd of May, the Teslic/Doboj route was quite free and the traffic went unobstructed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we get to May 1st, at least then you will agree that there was fighting in the area, that it was not easy to get between Teslic and Tesanj, or Teslic and Doboj; that kind of movement was restricted. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the decision of the 4th of April, taken by the Teslic Municipal Assembly, at the time, the road was open and one could, after the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd of May, the Serb forces took over Doboj. Doboj was completely under the Serb control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about whether or not Doboj was under Serb control. I'm talking about the road, the road between Doboj and Teslic. So in the summer of 1992 - we can start May 1st if you'd like - isn't it correct that one could not travel easily and directly by the old direct road between Teslic and Doboj? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even when you left in April of 1992, you couldn't use the open roads. There were checkpoints along the way, all along the way. People would have stopped you, so you went through the woods, the forest, with a guide; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In April 1992, I was in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When you left Teslic is what I was trying to direct you to. I know you're very precise and I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, ten days was like ten years, believe me. I left on the 26th of May, 1992. Let me just help you with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you left, it was impossible for communication to Tesanj and you could not have gone directly to Doboj from Teslic either; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I have said. There were barricades on the road towards Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I really just have two more areas and then I'm going to turn you over to Ms. Korner. I wanted to know about the turning in of weapons. Because I looked at your answer from yesterday. You said: I got that pistol legally from the secretary of the secretariat of National Defence, and I had a permit for that weapon in my official capacity. This is how I understand official capacity, Mr. Osmanovic, and it may be the interpretation. Is it correct that you were given that pistol and could hold it legally because you were secretary of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when you were no longer the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, under that same reasoning, you had no official capacity and still you continued to hold that pistol; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just the last thing: You stated that in early May or late April, Major Bosanac of the JNA Djulici barracks was replaced by Major Dejan Bilanovic, also a JNA officer, who was also appointed as the commander of the TO, and you added: This appointment had to be from a high level of the JNA. Can you just tell me what you meant by that or why you concluded that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Bilanovic and Bosanac were professional officers of the JNA, and it was only the JNA that had the authority to deploy them in a certain area or to assign them to a new post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I probably won't be able to speak with you later, but I wish you a good journey back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Baruch. Ms. Korner, I suppose you have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have a couple, Your Honour. Three, one of which may take longer and I'm going to work backwards. Re-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The list that is shown in that newspaper, Mr. Osmanovic, I'd like you -- it was put to you, and that's absolutely correct that the list itself does not state that people are to be liquidated. But I want to go through the people on that list and see if you can tell me what happened to them. Can we start, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I submit that that is not relevant to the events of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: -- the time that he has testified for because he talked about the list as his motivation for leaving Teslic, and now they are going into future events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I disagree completely with you, Madam Baruch. What we are talking about, you tried to contest the witness's judgement that this was a hit list, and I myself was going to ask the same question that has now been put by Ms. Korner, precisely because I want to get more information from the witness to see whether he had -- could reasonably have come to that conclusion. And the only way he could come to that conclusion was either he was told that it was a hit list at the time, or he can go through the list one by one and tell us whether any or how many of these people were liquidated. Because the article also says which it turns out the Mice paramilitary formation used as a kind of reference point in June 1992. So I am going to allow the question. Of course if you want to put on record your objection in more detail you are free to do so. But I'm not only going to allow it but I was going to put it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that you might -- it might be relevant as to whether or not his thoughts on that occasion turned out to be correct or not correct. However, with regard to his motivation for leaving, it doesn't matter if his judgement was right or wrong. It matters whether he made that judgement at that time. Now, he said he has made that judgement, but if somebody died in 1993, it certainly would have no relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Baruch, there are two points which were made, one which you have just referred to. The other one you tried to extract from the witness's mouth a declaration that possibly he was wrong and he had no reasonable ground on which to base his conclusion that this was a hit list. Irrespective of whether he considered it a hit list at the time he came to know about it, you contested his appreciation or his evaluation of this list as being -- and described it as a hit list and you contested that. You said there is nothing on the basis of which he could reach that conclusion. And we have every, every responsibility to go through this list now to see whether, even now, talking of the events 10 or 12 years later, this was indeed a hit list. Because you contested that this was a hit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And this Court has also mentioned some men, Mice, who I'm sure this Court is aware this witness was not in Teslic during that time, and that's a whole other area that if he's going to be able to explore, I would ask for the opportunity to explore Mice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask him about Mice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mice was mentioned in the article, not by the witness or by me or -- I just referred to it because it's mentioned in the article. Yes, Ms. Korner. Please proceed with the question, and if possible, if necessary, we go through the list one by one. Because I intended to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to do so and I intend to do so without referring to the names, if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go through that list, please, Mr. Osmanovic. Number 1: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: We have a date here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean, you have a date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May we have a date, if he knows what happened to the man, the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Give us as much detail as you can, Mr. Osmanovic, as to what happened to this man or to this person, and when. I assume that he couldn't have died or disappeared or anything happened to him before this list was allegedly compiled, so we're talking from the period when, according to you, this list was compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can answer, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sunija Ahmetasevic was ill-treated in a camp. He was beaten up. He was then exchanged. He now resides and works in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... where he resides. Telling us that he was then exchanged is enough, and I don't think we need to go beyond that and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when he was arrested and placed in a camp, roughly? What year, I think is the best.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 2 on the list, the brother of the first.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He resided in Stenjak and he left before this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about numbers 4 and 5?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also went -- they went and they stayed in a camp for a while. They were detained there and then they were ill-treated and then exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, the year?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think to say that only tell us the year if it's not 1992. Number 6?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I need to read out the name or is -- should I simply say that I don't know the person?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need to read out the name, and just say you don't know the person if you don't.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the person. He is a Croat. He was also ill-treated in a camp and he was exposed to tortures of all sorts. That was in 1992. He managed to leave, and leave for Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 7?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 8?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to him either.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He managed to leave in May 1992 and he arrived in Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 12?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person was 70 when people were being arrested. He was in a concentration camp during the Second World War. He was in a concentration camp in 1992. He was ill-treated there and then he was exchanged. Again, this was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 13 and number 16. I'm not quite sure why, but ...

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 13, the person who managed to leave in early May 1992, left the territory of Teslic. But here it says 13 and 16, but there is no second name here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, number 14 is you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, when it was written, when the list was compiled, would that have been before you went to Tesanj? Almost certainly, looking at the description.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that I received, this was before I left Teslic municipality, and this was one of the reasons for which I finally left it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Number 15, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, 16 -- number 17?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or 18?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the person. He was my neighbour. He also managed to leave in May 1992 and move to Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was detained in a camp, tortured, and managed to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 22?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. In early May, this person left Teslic for Croatia. That was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honour wants me to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. I want to finish this list completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. This person was also detained in a camp, exposed to torture, still suffers health problems. He was exchanged, and before that he ended up in a detention camp in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The compiler of the list, or the information, appeared to think that the fact that this man had a green bathroom was relevant. Do you know why that would be? Why would a green bathroom be of relevance to an intelligence gatherer?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I've got to object. This man says he was -- he himself was not an intelligence gatherer, so he has to speculate not only what a person might believe about it, but also what a person who was an intelligence gatherer might attribute to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Is it important to proceed with this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is -- well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's only relevant insofar as the author of this seems to have thrown an innuendo that, you know, the colour of one's bathroom was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I think it is, Your Honour. Let me put it this -- I'm sorry. I interrupted you, Judge Janu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your knowledge of Serbs, what significance did the colour green have to them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In everyday conversations in Bosnia, one could hear that the green represents Muslims or Bosniaks, sometimes jokingly. This was sometimes said jokingly. But the green colour was associated with Bosniaks, with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Number 24, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also a person who was detained in various camps, one of them being the public security station, exchanged in late 1992; before that, ill-treated in various camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 25?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Identical as the person under 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. That's not quite clear. Do you mean the same thing happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely the same things happened to him in June 1992. He was arrested, detained in a camp, ill-treated, beaten up, and then exchanged in late June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then number 26?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. This person managed to leave the territory of Teslic municipality before the arrests took place. That was before May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 28 -- 27?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. He was arrested, detained in a concentration camp, beaten, ill-treated, and exchanged in late June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the next one appears to be his brother.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again the same case. Both of them were in a camp. They were ill-treated, they were tortured, and they were exchanged together in late June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then number 29? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this person, but I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 30?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this person. He managed to leave in May 1992, before the arrests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 32?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was also arrested, detained in a concentration camp, beaten, and remained in Teslic all this time. After the end of the war, he died, although he was still a very young person.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know enough about this person.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him. I'm not sure who he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 33, 34, 35, and possibly 36 are Croats, am I right, or Muslims? Without reading the names, would they be Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 33 is a Croat. 34 is -- I don't know. It's hard for me to tell by the family name. 35 is a Bosniak. 36 is somebody I know. He's a Croat. He was also detained in various camps and ill-treated, and I'm not sure what happened to him, but I believe that he has remained in Teslic. He was not exchanged and he never arrived in Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was also arrested in June 1992. He was then detained in a camp and exchanged in late June 1992.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we apparently go to 51. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 52, 53, 54, 55, I'm not sure what that means, but ... 56?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then some extra names. These are all the people, I think, that -- or two, the first two certainly you've told us about. What happened to number 1?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or number 2?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2, he was arrested, ended up in a camp, suffered torture, ill-treatment. He was beaten up. Then he was exchanged sometime in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3 there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my work colleague. I believe that he managed to leave Teslic and go to Croatia, sometime in April or May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 4?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was a very influential person who ended up in a camp. He was ill-treated there and tortured, and he is a person who is still missing. Nobody knows his lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't propose to follow with the last -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I think appropriately now, just exhibit the original handwritten version that we have, which will become 1960. It was disclosed to the Defence in B/C/S in December 2001, but the translation only came on Monday. So I wonder if that could be handed out. Your Honour, I don't -- there's no point, I think, in showing it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May I see a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I tell you how we acquired it? Because it's not on --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I would object to that as being testimony for which she doesn't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's not being -- I don't think you're offering, yes, offering it as testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm offering, but I can get Mr. Inayat to tell us where it came from. But if Ms. Baruch doesn't want to know, then I'm not at all bothered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Korner. Then if it's necessary to get Mr. Inayat, we will get him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was supplied to us as a result of a request made by us to the Bosnian embassy in March of 2001, and there is an indication from them where it comes from, but if Ms. Baruch objects to that, then I won't lead that. But that's how we came into possession of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this you want to give exhibit number what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P1960, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to it, it's not exactly the same as the list that is P1959. It was not something seen by this witness, apparently, and I would object to it being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection overruled, Madam Baruch. And you are free later on at any time to ask questions about this document, and if necessary, Ms. Korner, please bring over Mr. Inayat or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- whoever it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if there are differences in the list, and I notice one, for example, being the name of the last person --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are differences. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can notice quite a few at first sight, but it doesn't mean to say that because of that this is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I don't know what it's being admissible for, as this witness never saw it, it wasn't published in the newspaper, and I don't believe that Ms. Korner is qualified to testify to the Court with regard to anything about this list. And so yes, we have that objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not testifying about this. But the normal demand is to know where documents come from when we produce them, and I'm simply short-circuiting having to put Mr. Inayat into the witness box to say that. But as I said, I'm perfectly happy to do that. As to its admissibility, it is a document which mentions this witness's name and another witness's name, with a description, and we say it's admissible in exactly the same way as all other documents which come from this area are admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The discussion is closed on this. It's being admitted, subject to the usual caveat, and marked as P1960. Do you have any further questions on re-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I've just got one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, you were asked about the disarmament order, which said all paramilitaries, and you said over and over again that it only applied to non-Serbs. You told us yesterday about barricades being manned by paramilitaries. Were those paramilitaries, those Serb paramilitaries, disarmed as a result of the order?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got to object to this, because the order was that they should turn it in. So if she is asking whether they obeyed the order, this witness didn't obey the order. Many people didn't obey the order, and it would have no relevance to whether or not they were included in the order. So I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can answer the question, Mr. Osmanovic. If you do not know, say so, please.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These barricades were where the paramilitary formations were. Yes, they were armed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's 10.30. Before we can -- how many more questions do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was my last question, but I've got a couple of what's sometimes called housekeeping matters to deal with on documents. Your Honour, I'm perfectly happy to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, because I can't keep the interpreters and everyone here if you have some points to raise. Judge Janu has some questions to put and I have some questions to put. So we'll break for 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay, but I had a meeting which had been scheduled and which went beyond what I had expected. So as all meetings do, or most meetings do. Yes, Ms. Korner. Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just to get back to that last question,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Serb paramilitaries at the barricades were armed. Are you aware whether or not, as a result of this order by the Crisis Staff, those arms were handed in or they were in any way disarmed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not disarmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Osmanovic. There was another gentleman with a similar name, but slightly different. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, Judge Janu has a few questions for you. Judge Janu, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, Mr. Osmanovic, you told us that replacement of the communist system was a great delight for the citizens, and you also told us that interethnic relations were indeed on a high level. My first question is: Were you a member of the League of Communists or were you brought up in the family where the membership -- where was the membership of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never a member of communists, nor was any of my proper family, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my second question: In your statement, there is that you graduated in Pristina university in art and languages, and in one of the exhibits we just went through here, was that you graduated from Islamic university of Cairo. Did you graduate of both of these universities or the information in exhibit P1959 is not correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only have the diploma of the faculty of philosophy in Pristina, so the other information is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And after your graduation, you served as an imam. Excuse me my low knowledge, but it is the same position as hodza?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And people who have no religious education can serve in this function?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have secondary education. There are also faculties of theology, which is higher education. Those who do not complete the secondary theological schools cannot work as imams or as hodzas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So there's a misunderstanding. My feeling was that you completed the philosophical university, languages and art, and my question was: If the person without religious education can serve as an imam or hodza.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No religious school -- I mean, do you include there secondary education as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So your secondary education was religious?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as an imam with the secondary education, which I did complete, and I could do it even without a university diploma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. I understand now. So you have secondary education in a religious area also? Yes. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I would like to -- in April 1993, you gave interview to Teslicke Informativne Novine and you said there two things. I will cite it from the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like us to give him a copy of it? We have one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So it's the second page, first line, first line and the third line. And you said: The aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina was prepared much earlier. And in third line you said: The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was prepared outside of the country. So my first question is: Can you tell us, can you clarify for us on what basis did you form this conclusion? And after that I will have another question concerning this.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave this interview in April 1993, when the war was raging in Bosnia-Herzegovina and when it was already quite clear what had happened in the territory of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Yugoslav, the so-called Yugoslav People's Army, and the paramilitary formations, in 60 days after the beginning of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, took 70 per cent of its territory. No -- only an organised, well-equipped military force was not needed to do it [as interpreted]. It could only be done by the so-called Yugoslav People's Army, following the well-established script which, to my mind, was conceived in Belgrade. In the course of the 60 days, 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina was placed under the control of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my second question to this subject is a little bit speculative, but anyway, I would like your opinion on it, if you are able to give it to me. Without these actions from outside, do you think you would -- at that time, you would be able to solve the problems by yourself, without all this bloodshed? In other way, do you think that you were able to, without this intervention, to find a way how to live Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. together peacefully?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my last question: Because you are -- you have religious education and you serve in this area, and you also have a long political career, how would you estimate -- what's your opinion about the role of churches, Islamic, Catholic, and the third one, Orthodox, what was the role of churches in this conflict, Bosnian conflict?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the religious communities did not contribute significantly to the deterioration of interethnic relations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some people say that it was a religious war, but I never saw a religious official head any army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. If that's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Mr. Osmanovic. Do you know Fadil Isic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fadil Isic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fadil Isic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1992, he had a heart attack and was put in a hospital, or rather, the health centre in Teslic, and has been missing ever since. To this day, after several exhumations in Teslic, his remains have not been found. And he was responsible for finances in the local organisation of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question. Was he a member of the SDA? And you have answered that. Do you know someone by the name of Botic, who was also an SDA member? And if you do, can you tell us what his first name was.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Now, what his name was, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened to him? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, after concentration camps, he was killed and all trace of him is lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my first question -- my next question to you: From the list that you had seen, being the translation of what had appeared in that newspaper, the Nezavisne how many of those persons were SDA members? Were the majority of the Muslim SDA members listed in that document or not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most of them were not members of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why would, according to you, these two names not figure in the list that you were shown today? You assume that these two persons have been killed, eliminated, from what I gather, while, according to what you told us, none of the persons that appeared on the list, with the exception of Rasim Galijasevic, were killed. Why would 56 or 60 persons -- 59 persons out of a list of what would be a hit list not be eliminated and two persons that are not on the hit list be eliminated?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that those who decided to publish this also had in mind those who were liquidated after they were taken to concentration camps, and perhaps that is why they decided not to go into full detail when listing the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Fadil Isic does appear on the other list that you handed later on in the day, document -- Exhibit P1960. But he does not appear on the -- he appears there as number 44. A certain Dibic, do you know a certain person by the name of Dibic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be Gibic, with a "G."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened to this person that you know by the name of Gibic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, all trace of that person is lost. That person was not born in Teslic. He taught all National Defence in school and he was never a member of the Party of Democratic Action. However, after detention and stay in concentration camps, that person went missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And a certain person by the name of Glancer?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that person well, so that I'd rather not say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in your statement to the Prosecution, to the Prosecutor, you did affirm that he was one of the three persons killed in Teslic. Do you stand by that statement or do you want to retract it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I am not sure I can talk about Glancer right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you do agree with me that none of these two persons appear on the list that you were shown earlier on today, neither Gibic nor Glancer?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in this newspaper text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, going back: Fadil Isic, Botic, Gibic, Glancer, was any one of those four politically active at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fadil Isic, as I have said, was the cashier in the local SDA, and he was also a councilman in the Municipal Assembly. And Botic was also another activist of the SDA. The others were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that closes that. Now, you did explain to us yesterday, or described to us yesterday, events when the JNA tried to take possession of the records, and you said that the attempt was not successful because people gathered in front of the building and blocked the way to the JNA. What was the size of the gathering and what was the ethnicity of the gathering?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were somewhere between 200 to 250 people in front of the building, and since they were urban dwellers who had received information about those activities, they were of all ethnicities, Bosniaks and Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my question actually was directed to knowing whether there were any Serbs in the gathering, in the group.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you were referring to this JNA attempt to take possession of the documents of the Defence, whatever it was, you mentioned - and I'm referring you now not just to your testimony but also to your statement - that you had learned from a certain Degirmandzic that the JNA had arrived in Teslic and tried to take these records by force. But you also said there were similar attempts in other municipalities, such as Gracanica and Lukavac and these forcible seizures of the military records were shown on television. But I want to know from you if you are in a position to give us an answer is: In the case of Gracanica, who -- what ethnicity was the person responsible for the keeping -- for the safekeeping of those records? We heard that in the case of Teslic it was a Muslim. In the case of Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the case of Lukavac?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know of any other place where the JNA made similar attempts?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was - how shall I put it? - a general attempt to take over records from the national or the defence secretariats by the JNA. I presume such an order was issued, and it was happening in a larger number of municipalities, and there were problems where the Bosniak and Croat population constituted a majority, that is, where the municipal presidents were Bosniaks and Croats, that is, where there was a resistance. I quoted to you two municipalities, because I could follow the developments there directly, owing to electronic media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where would the headquarters, national headquarters, of the secretariat of the People's Defence be at the time? Which city?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that would be where?
