utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo. Are you in a position to tell us whether in Sarajevo they would have had exactly the same or a copy, or if not the original of the records that were also kept in Teslic? In other words, I'm putting it to you that the records that were kept in Teslic were also kept elsewhere, at least in the headquarters of the ministry of People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Ministry of Defence had under it National Defence secretariats in municipalities, and it didn't keep the records of all the municipalities in its own archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not even the JNA would have copies of those records?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And not even Belgrade would there be copies of those?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a completely separate structure. On the one hand, you have civilian authorities who took note of records, mobilisation, and so on and so forth; and on the other, you had the military structure, and that was completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was important for us to know. I don't think I have any further questions. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask one thing arising out of Judge Janu's questions in respect of the religious personnel involvement? The answer was: No religious person led the military, and I want to ask -- was involved with the military. I want to ask if any religious person in Teslic was involved in political life.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I don't see how that relates to the question about religious people heading the military, which was an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did answer that question. No. Let's leave it at that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, that's not what Judge Janu's question was. She wanted to know not whether they were involved in the military. But whether religious leaders, and I'd have to go back, I haven't got the LiveNote. The answer was not leading the military. That's an incomplete answer, in my respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it is obvious that the witness, according to the witness, the involvement of the religious was not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I invite Your Honour to look at his statement, please, at page 9, the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll read it out to him and I will put a different question myself. Mr. Osmanovic, in your statement to the Prosecutor, you said: "There was an orthodox priest by the name of Savo Knezevic, who was a deputy to the assembly for Bosnia and Herzegovina when the Serbian republic was formed he joined the Serbian republic. He was in Teslic and was a very influential person in Teslic. I do not know if he was part of the Crisis Staff or not." Would this make you change your statement earlier on in reply to Judge Janu's question, or would you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: ADIL OSMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would adhere to my previous answer. According to the laws that were in force at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the first general elections, clerics [Realtime transcript read in error "clerks"] were not banned from engaging in politics. They were not prevented from becoming deputies in various assemblies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could I just correct the note while I see it. He said clerics or the witness said clerics.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The translation was clerics and it has come over as clerks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He said clerics. I heard him say clerics or at least I heard -- yes. Mr. Osmanovic, that brings us to an end of your testimony here. The only remaining thing for me to say is to thank you for having come over and give evidence in this trial. You will now be ushered out of this courtroom and given all the attention you need and assistance you need to enable you to return to your residence, to your home country. And on behalf of the Tribunal, Judge Janu and everyone present here, we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Organisational matters of any left?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, it relates back to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it relates back to the four documents in the Petrovac binder, where we couldn't trace the origin. Mr. Inayat, by dint of a great deal of research, has in fact found identical documents from a source that we can trace, and what we've done is we've altered the schedule, the list, accordingly, and we've put together a new list together with the same documents from a different source which we can trace, and I can borrow the one for the moment. It came -- and it should be very familiar to Mr. Ackerman, one of them. It was given by one of the Delalic counsel to us, which is a case that Mr. Ackerman was in, I think, his first case here. And Your Honour will see where the rest of them come from. It's been highlighted. So it's the same. As Your Honours knows, we filed documents, the same documents from different sources. So we're replacing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure that the ones that were handed in before are withdrawn, because they would have an ERN number, and that the new ones are placed instead. And again, I reserve -- Ms. Baruch, you don't need to answer today. I mean you can -- I give you time to consult with Mr. Ackerman on this and then you come back to us tomorrow when we meet again. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I think for the moment that's all -- oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Your Honour, we perhaps ought to make the article that Judge Janu read to the witness an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it necessary? I don't think it is necessary, because she referred to two points only, and I don't think we need the article in the records.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If anybody wants to go and have a look at the article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going on the normal suggestion from the Defence that without an exhibit number it's not possible to trace the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was just a simple question. You stated in this article, you made two affirmations, two statements. Could you give us an explanation. Do we need to have the article as well? I mean, I don't know. I mean, we can have it. It's another two pages, four pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: No. I think that the witness would be a person to make it an exhibit, and I accept that Judge Janu used and spoke the precise section about which she was interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't see how the witness makes the document an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's probably because Ms. Baruch is not completely familiar with the system here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite happy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wouldn't be put -- brought forward by the witness. And if it is, it would be handed to the Prosecution and made a Prosecution Exhibit or whatever, or a Defence Exhibit, as we go along. We've had instances of the witness bringing forward documents which the -- were shown to the Defence and then the Defence was allowed to exhibit them as a Defence Exhibit. And similarly, it worked out the opposite way as well. But we work in a different manner maybe than what you are used to. I mean, so... If you insist on having it tendered in evidence, I can't say no. I was just drawing your attention as to whether it's absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say that it's not normally me who tries to put documents into evidence, but the constant moan, if I can put it that way, is that unless the document has an exhibit number in the transcript, nobody knows what it is later on. So I'm easy. As far as I'm concerned, if Your Honours don't want to make it an exhibit, I don't particularly want to make it an exhibit either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will not contrast you any further, Ms. Korner. You want to make it an exhibit, we will give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be P1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other than that, Your Honour, I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow we are going to have Mr. Sebire. Do you have an idea how long he we will be here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't. Ms. Richterova is going to call him. But what we intend to do, given that there can be no cross-examination until Tuesday, is not just get him to produce the schedules but actually deal with some -- there is a video, for example, of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one of the exhumations which shows a number of other things as well. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The pleasure is yet to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The pleasure is yet to come, Your Honour. But anyhow, I would think probably the best part of tomorrow's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May I ask if we have a schedule of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's going to be provided after court to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Today? Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time to just put into the record that our interpreter has informed us that on LiveNote, page 40, line 7, the witness has said force was needed to do it, not force was not needed to do it. And if that complies with the oral record, then I would just ask that that correction be made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It's an obvious mistake to me. It's an obvious mistake to me. Ms. Korner, Madam Baruch, Mr. Cunningham, I should like you to, by tomorrow, organise yourselves a little bit, particularly you, Ms. Korner, with regard to the binder documents as such, because basically we have admitted in evidence bits and pieces of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought you had admitted the whole Teslic binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We hadn't admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely what I have been asking you to organise for tomorrow. If you are in a position to do that now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Organise what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: See what has been already admitted, what hasn't been admitted, whether you want all the rest to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I did ask, when it was dealt with, when you raised the objections of Mr. Ackerman, and my response was that I asked for the whole binder to be admitted, the objections notwithstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we stuck only on those two or three documents that were referred to in the first paragraph of Mr. Ackerman's response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I replied to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We never really ruled that all the others were being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour kindly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So they are being admitted now. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can adjourn until tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
